cells.tense: You are tending what matters right now, with both hands on it.
cells.ask: Name one thing you keep alive that would notice if you stopped, and say so out loud to one person today.
cells.core:
You're doing the quiet work of keeping something alive, and you're in the room while you do it. Nothing frantic about it. You know what needs water and what needs waiting, and you make the call again each morning. People around you can feel that steadiness, even when they can't name it.

What keeps this clean is that you can tell carrying from clutching. When a season ends, you let it end, and the ending doesn't feel like failure. You keep space for whoever's in front of you without needing them to stay. That's the balance you're here to feed — not more effort, just more room to breathe around it.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it alive without holding it too tight.
cells.place: in the company of the person right in front of you

cells.tense: You are bracing for a season that hasn't arrived yet and may never.
cells.ask: Pick the one thing that actually needs you today and let the other two wait until tomorrow without touching them.
cells.core:
You're caring for people who haven't asked yet. Before anyone wants anything, you've already arranged yourself around what they might need — the visit, the money, the version of the conversation that won't go well. Most of that care is landing on days that don't exist.

Somewhere behind this is a picture of how it all works out, and you're working toward it harder than anyone asked. The trouble is the work has stopped being about the person and started being about staying ahead. What this balance is for is care that doesn't exhaust you. That's possible. It starts when you stop carrying loads nobody handed you.
cells.sheetLine: You're bracing for a season you haven't reached.
cells.place: in the company of the person right in front of you

cells.tense: You stopped tending a while back and left the gate closed behind you.
cells.ask: Start with something smaller than a person — one plant, one shared meal — and keep it going for a week.
cells.core:
The work of tending stopped. You're not cruel about it — you're careful. You stay just past arm's length from the people you used to keep room for, and you've gotten good at making that look like nothing in particular.

What's not gone is the ability to see what a thing needs and when. You just stopped stepping toward it. Doing one small tending thing with your own hands is enough to start — the ground under you starts to feel like ground again, and there's no need to force feeling into the spot that's been quiet. The stepping returns with the doing, week by week, on its own schedule.
cells.sheetLine: The care is still there. The stepping stopped.
cells.place: in the company of the person right in front of you

cells.tense: You are already holding people together and calling it nothing you did.
cells.ask: Say out loud, to one of them, that you did the thing — the arranging, the remembering, the showing up.
cells.core:
Half the people you know are steadier because of you, and you'd rarely say that. You remember the birthdays, you read the room, you're the one who called first. You just file it under how things went rather than something you did.

What's absent isn't the care. It's the credit. Somebody has to say the work counted, and that somebody is you. When you name it plainly, you start to see where it's costing you and where it's fine. This balance is about release that comes from finishing, not from defeat. The first thing to finish is the pretending that none of this was your hand.
cells.sheetLine: You did it. You're the only one who hasn't said so.
cells.place: in the company of the person right in front of you
